summary: This paper presents gate-based quantum option pricing using amplitude estimation for a European call option, with simulator results for m = 3, 5, 7, 9 sampling qubits and a noisy IBM Q Tokyo demonstration using 3 qubits, 8192 shots per run, and 20 repeated runs. The hardware experiment uses readout mitigation and CNOT-error extrapolation, but the paper does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage over classical Monte Carlo; it remains a small-scale proof of concept.

experiments.description: Amplitude-estimation pricing of a European call option on a 2-qubit discretized log-normal underlying, evaluated on a simulator for multiple sampling-qubit counts and compared against classical Monte Carlo.

algorithm.variant: standard amplitude estimation with QFT phase estimation

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 2-qubit discretization of the underlying spot price distribution; basis states represent four discretized asset values loaded into a quantum register, then a comparator and controlled Y-rotation encode the call payoff.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate E[max(0, S_T - K)] via amplitude estimation.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Comparator qubit marks whether S_T >= K; payoff encoded through piecewise controlled Y-rotations.

problem_instance.description: European call option on a single underlying asset with log-normal terminal distribution.

dataset_specification.description: Black-Scholes-Merton synthetic distribution; 4-point discretization over [1.21, 1.74, 2.28, 2.81] for the hardware section, and a separate 3-qubit illustrative distribution in Fig. 3 for simulation figures.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Truncate the log-normal distribution to three standard deviations around the mean; discretize to 2 qubits for hardware experiments.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Amplitude estimation run for m in {3,5,7,9} on simulator; compare estimated option price to analytical BSM value; figure shows convergence behavior.

implementation_details.classical_solver: classical Monte Carlo and analytical Black-Scholes-Merton benchmark
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Load log-normal distribution and construct payoff circuit.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Map measured y to a=sin^2(yπ/M) and recover option price from scaling relation.

results.unit: O(M^-1/2) in classical Monte Carlo samples M

speedup_claims.conditions: standard amplitude estimation with QFT phase estimation; assuming ideal quantum resources
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper notes that the full AE circuits are far from current and near-term hardware; the quadratic speedup is asymptotic and not a wall-clock guarantee.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(M^-1) in terms of quantum samples M for standard amplitude estimation

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; only simulator convergence plots for m = 3, 5, 7, 9 and a toy 2-qubit uncertainty register are reported.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Standard amplitude estimation with phase estimation would require more qubits and deeper circuits; the paper reports only simulator results for a small European call example and compares against Monte Carlo analytically.
limiting_factors: No demonstrated runtime advantage over classical methods
Circuit depth and qubit overhead for full AE are substantial

notes: Hardware is a simulator in Fig. 8; the exact simulator type is not named, so simulator_other is inferred.

The paper reports m sampling qubits and a 2-qubit uncertainty register for the hardware experiment, but does not state a single total qubit count for the simulator figure; num_qubits is therefore left null/inferred only at the register level in the description.
Circuit depth for this simulator experiment is not explicitly reported.
The paper presents simulator convergence for a European call option and compares against classical Monte Carlo/BSM, but does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Amplitude-estimation pricing of a European call option on IBM Q Tokyo using a 3-qubit circuit and maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation without phase estimation, with readout mitigation and CNOT-error mitigation across multiple initial spot prices.

algorithm.variant: amplitude estimation without phase estimation / maximum-likelihood estimation (Suzuki et al.)
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Angles for the distribution-loading rotations are varied with S0; payoff angles fixed by c=0.25.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 2 qubits encode the discretized underlying distribution; 1 qubit encodes the payoff. Uniformly controlled Y-rotations implement the piecewise linear payoff.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate E[max(0, S_T - K)] using amplitude estimation without phase estimation.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Piecewise payoff encoded directly into the ancilla qubit; no explicit constraints beyond the payoff circuit.

problem_instance.description: European call option on a single underlying asset with varying initial spot price.

dataset_specification.description: Log-normal BSM distribution with 4 discretized values [1.21, 1.74, 2.28, 2.81].

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Truncate to three standard deviations around the mean; map to 2 qubits; vary only the initial spot price across eight experiments.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Each experiment run on IBM Q Tokyo with 8192 shots, repeated 20 times; average measured probabilities over the 20 runs; compare mitigated and unmitigated estimates to exact option prices.

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise; readout error and two-qubit gate errors
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: readout error mitigation via 8x8 calibration matrix; Richardson extrapolation / CNOT error amplification using 1x, 3x, 5x CNOT replacements

implementation_details.transpilation_target: IBM Q Tokyo connectivity with qubits 6, 10, 11
implementation_details.classical_solver: classical Monte Carlo and exact option price benchmark

transpilation_settings.routing_method: no swaps required due to full connectivity of chosen qubits

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Construct 2-qubit log-normal distribution and payoff angles; calibrate readout matrix.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Maximum-likelihood estimation over measured probabilities for k=0,1; Richardson extrapolation to zero-noise limit; recover option price from estimated amplitude.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: option price estimates track exact values after mitigation; unmitigated estimates biased low/high depending on S0

speedup_claims.conditions: amplitude estimation without phase estimation / maximum-likelihood estimation; asymptotic in number of quantum samples
speedup_claims.caveats: The hardware experiment is noisy and uses only m=1; the paper emphasizes that this does not make the algorithm immediately compatible with noisy devices, but it shortens circuits relative to standard AE.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(M^-1) in terms of quantum samples for amplitude estimation; hardware experiment uses m=1 (Q applications k=0,1)

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; the hardware experiment uses only 3 qubits and m = 1 (k = 0,1) for a toy European call instance.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: A 3-qubit IBM Q Tokyo experiment with 8192 shots and 20 repetitions, plus readout mitigation and CNOT-error mitigation; no end-to-end advantage over classical pricing is shown.
limiting_factors: No demonstrated speedup over classical Monte Carlo
Quadratic AE speedup is not enough to overcome hardware overhead

notes: IBM Q Tokyo and 8192 shots are explicitly reported.
The paper reports 18 CNOT gates and 33 single-qubit gates for the optimized QA|0>3 circuit, but not a total depth for the hardware experiment; circuit depth is therefore not reported.
The 3-qubit count is explicit from the text (two uncertainty qubits plus one payoff qubit).
The paper reports noisy hardware execution on IBM Q Tokyo with mitigation, but the results are a proof-of-principle rather than a demonstrated advantage.
